items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: When the House resumes on
Tuesday, 12 November the Government intends  to progress the Members of Parliament
(Remuneration and Services) Bill, the Health  and Safety (Pike River Implementation)
Bill, and the New Zealand International Convention Centre Bill. Wednesday is a
members’ day.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: I wonder whether I can
inquire of the Leader of the House whether he has any intention to introduce a bill in the
coming couple of weeks around the reform of the Teachers Council.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I have not seen that bill in the
legislative process, but that does not mean th at it may not be coming up in the next 2
weeks. I am sorry I cannot be more specific.
Canterbury, Recovery—Offer on Red Zone Properties
1. DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First)  to the Minister for Canterbury Earthquake

items.speaker: Recovery
items.text: Is he satisfied with progress on all aspects of the Canterbury earthquake
recovery?
No. Although there are many good things happ ening, there are also many things that
could progress more speedily.
Denis O’Rourke: How can he be satisfied, if he is, or not, when the court has found
that his Government’s residential red zone  land clearance offers were unlawful on
grounds of improper process?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: It is an interesting ques tion, given my answer, so I
will repeat it for him. No. Although there ar e many things that are going well, there are
others that could be progressing more speedily.
Denis O’Rourke: How could he be satisfied when the result of th e red zone land—
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member has every right to ask his supplementary
question.
Denis O’Rourke: It is good to hear that there is so much—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Just ask it.
Denis O’Rourke : How could he be satisfied when the result of the red zone land
clearance process, using an outdated and hit-and-miss 2007 rating valuation, gave a few
red-zoners a windfall but many more of them  such large losses that they could not
afford to buy another home?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Of the more than 7,000 flat land red zone clients, well
over 6,900 have entered into sale and purchas e agreements with the Government, and
many others are in that pro cess. I think that speaks for itself. Those people were in a
dreadful position. They have been given an opportunity to move on with their lives.
Denis O’Rourke : How could he possibly be satisfied when the Government’s
inexplicable decision to offer only 50 pe rcent of the outdated 2007 rating value to
owners of residential bare land and to uninsured property owners has also been declared
14478 Questions for Oral Answer 7 Nov 2013
unlawful by the court because the Government did not use the powers or follow the
process required by the Canterbury Earthqu ake Recovery Act, as required and as
intended by Parliament?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: That is a matter that is currently before the courts, so I
do not think it would be in the public interest for me to engage in a discussion of what at
the end of the day is Mr O’Rourke’s own opinion.
Denis O’Rourke: How could the Minister be even remotely satisfied with the deeply
unpopular and badly performing Earthquake  Commission, especially when it
gerrymanders its survey results by marki ng 31,000 out of 154,000 claimants with “do
not survey” tags?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I clearly said that there were some things I am not
satisfied with, and I have today asked the State Services Commissioner to conduct a full
review of that particular issue so that we  can have confidence in the surveys of the
Earthquake Commission.

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: Has the Minister asked for or received any advice on an
alternative to red zone financial settlements for those who are still waiting for the Port
Hills zoning review decisions, which were due before Christmas last year; if so, will he
do something—anything—to fix the situation for them?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: There are 511 households on the Port Hills that are in
review. We had hoped to make an announcem ent about that, but the Quake Outcasts
decision would have meant that we were pur suing an offer that has for the time being
been determined as inappropriate. That would put us in contempt of court until we have
gone through the appeal process. There is not a lot that can be done at the present time. I
am deeply distressed by this, I have to say, and I do find it  extraordinary that someone
can sit on the bench of a court in this coun try and inflict such injustice on so many
people.

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! This is a point of order and it will be heard in silence.

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: I understand the issue that the Mini ster is faced with in terms of
the Quake Outcasts decision, which is w hy my question specif ically asked about
financial settlements as alternatives to red zone offers.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I listened carefully to the questi on and to the Minister’s answer. On
this occasion I believe the Minister addr essed the question. If the member is not
satisfied, the way to advance this issue is to ask further supplementary questions.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The Minister, in his answer,
denigrated the judiciary for the decision that it has brought down against his decision.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: No, I did not.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Yes, he did—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I am hearing a point of order.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: —and I would have thought that for him to, on the one hand,
refuse to answer a question from the primary questioner on the ground that this is before
the courts, and to then take a slap at the judge for laying down a lawful decision would
be outside the Standing Orders.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, I do not believe in any way that the issue was outside the
Standing Orders. It was for the Minister to be responsible fo r the answer that he gave.
He gave the answer and he bears responsibility for the way he answered the question.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I am sorry to belabour the
point, but Standing Order 114 does read: “A member may not use offensive words
against the House or against any member of  the judiciary.” I think Mr Brownlee was
right up against Standing Order 114 in what he  said there. There are, obviously, rules
7 Nov 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 14479
around the separation of powers here, and I think Standing Order 114 is very clear in its
nature.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Speaking further to that, the se cond point to be made is that
Standing Order 112 says: “(1) Matters awai ting or under adjudication … may not be
referred to …”. For the Minister to say that that was the reason he could not answer Mr
O’Rourke and to then put pressure upon the ju diciary by criticising it, effectively, in the
way that he did seems to me to be entir ely inconsistent, and, therefore, his later
comment must be out of order.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Again, I thank both members for th eir contributions. I think Grant
Robertson used words like “It was right up against the boundary”, or words to that
effect. I think that is a fair comment, but on this occasion the Minister has answered that
way, the statements have been made, and I am not going to rule them out of order. The
Minister has to accept responsibility for the answer he gave.

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: Will he take up the offer from the recently elected Mayor of
Christchurch, Lianne Dalziel, to work bett er together and get agreement between the
Canterbury Earthquake Recovery  Authority red zoning a nd the Christchurch City
Council’s section 124 notices so that people in green zoned but red-stickered homes can
get their lives back?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Yes.
Sexual Assault Allegations—Confidence in Police Investigation
2. JACINDA ARDERN (Labour)  to the Minister of Police : Does she have
confidence in the Police inve stigation of alleged sexual violation against young women
and underage girls in West Auckland?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I have confidence in the police.
Although the Police Commissioner has provided  me with assurance that the police
investigation has been thorough and appropriately managed, a number of questions have
been raised about this investigation. That  is why I have written to the Independent
Police Conduct Authority this morning, asking it to undertake an inquiry into this matter
and to provide me with an independent assurance that police have conducted this
investigation to the highest standard. Th e public of New Zealand needs to have
confidence that police take al legations of sexual assault ex tremely seriously and that
they will do all they can to ensure that perpetrators are held to account.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Why on Monday did she state that victims needed to come forward
in order for their cases to progress when it has been revealed now that several young
women and girls did exactly that, as long as 2 years ago?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Simply because the information that I had on Monday and
again on Tuesday was that although girls had been spoken to, they had not made formal
complaints. What was revealed last night was, in fact, that a young girl had made a
complaint. Neither the commissioner nor I was aware of that. That is one of the
questions that has been rais ed and one of the reasons I have asked the Independent
Police Conduct Authority specif ically to investigate the investigation of this young
girl’s complaint—who was 13—2 years ago.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Why was neither she, nor the Waitemat ā district commander, nor
the Police Commissioner properly briefed on this case at the very beginning?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I have expressed my disappointment this morning to the
commissioner that that has been the case. He is extremely disappoi nted that that has
been the case. My understanding is that he is conducting, with the district commander,
an inquiry into why that information was not available to them.
14480 Questions for Oral Answer 7 Nov 2013

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Is it her expectation that a person who makes a complaint of sexual
violation and gives information about their cl othing at the time of the incident would
then have it implied that what they were wearing could influence the case?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I really think that we should stop jumping to conclusions.
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! This was a legitimate question. It is a
serious matter, and I want to hear the answer.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: The police have very st rict protocols around the
investigation of sexual assault charges and allegations. It is  my expectation that police
will adhere to those. They have done a tremendous amount of work over the last years
to raise their performance to focus it on th e needs of victims. I would be extremely
disappointed if they had not lived up to thos e standards. That is one of the reasons I
have taken this so seriously that I have ta ken the unprecedented step of referring this to
the Independent Police Conduct Authority for investigation. I caution this House that
the investigations are ongoing and we should be very car eful that we do not say
anything that might prejudice bringing some of these young men to account.

items.speaker: Carol Beaumont
items.text: What efforts were made by the police over the last 2 years to warn
young women in west Auckland of the actions of this group, given its predatory nature
and well-signalled plans to target young women and to increase the number of young
men involved in its activities?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I am assured by the commissioner that this has been a
thorough and enthusiastic investigation by the police. They have been—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Enthusiastic?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Yes, the police are very ent husiastic to bring these young
men to account. It is my understanding that  the police have interviewed the young men
on numerous occasions and have spoken to their schools and the principals of those
schools.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: What about the girls’ schools?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: That is the information that the commissioner has given me.

items.speaker: But I repeat
items.text: the Independent Police Conduc t Authority will investigate the entire
investigation from 2 years ago, and it is important that politicians do not get involved in
that investigation, because it is a police operational issue. Th e Independent Police
Conduct Authority is the only one that can go through it minute by minute.

items.speaker: Carol Beaumont
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I actually asked what
efforts—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I heard the question, and on this occasion I invite the
member to repeat the question to the Minister.

items.speaker: Carol Beaumont
items.text: Thank you very much. What efforts were made by the police over
the last 2 years to warn young women in west  Auckland of the actions of this group,
given its predatory nature and well-signa lled plans to target young women and to
increase the number of young men involved in its activities?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Well, I thought I had just addressed that. The commissioner
has advised me that the police went to gr eat efforts to track down these young men and
speak with them and their families, and went and talked with their schools. The police
also talked with the parents of the girls,  but without any evidence, they cannot make
unsubstantiated accusations about young people.

items.speaker: Carol Beaumont
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. I still do not believe that
answers the question about warning young women in west Auckland.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! On this occasion, the Mini ster included the statement that
they had talked to the schools, et c., which obviously would have been—[ Interruption] I
have determined that on this  occasion the Minister has ad dressed the question. It may
7 Nov 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 14481
not be to the member’s satisfaction. The way forward is for the member to ask more
searching questions if she wants to.
Economic Programme—Progress
3. PAUL GOLDSMITH (National) to the Minister of Finance: What progress has
the National-led Government made in building a more productive and competitive
economy capable of supporting more jobs and higher incomes for New Zealanders?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associ ate Minister of Finance)  on behalf of the Minister
of Finance: The National-led Government was elected 5 years ago tomorrow, and I am
pleased to report that very considerable progr ess has been made in that time. In fact, on
just about every score the economy is in mu ch better shape than it was in late 2008.
Back then the economy had been shrinking fo r four quarters. In the past year the
economy grew by around 2.5 percent, one of th e highest rates in the OECD for that
year. This is helping to push business and c onsumer confidence to their highest level in
many years. Businesses are indicating strongly that they plan to invest more and hire
more staff over the coming year. This was confirmed in the employment data issued
yesterday.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: What other indicators confirm that  the economy is in better shape
than it was 5 years ago?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, there are many of them, and perhaps you could let me
run through just a few of them. Before our first Budget, Treasury to ld us that if we
continued with the previous policies, we woul d run deficits for ever  and net debt would
soar to over 60 percent of GDP by 2023  and never come down. Under this
Government’s responsible economic and fiscal management we are now on track to a
surplus in 2014-15. Net debt is expected to peak at below 30 percent of GDP despite the
$15 billion expected cost to the Crown of the Canterbury earthquakes. On the subject of
debt and deficits, back in 2008 the current account deficit was almost 9 percent of GDP
and New Zealand’s net external debt had blown out to 84 per cent of GDP. Now the
current account is 4.3 percent of GDP, less than half of what  it was 5 years ago, and net
external debt is 71 percent of GDP.

items.speaker: Te Ururoa Flavell
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Kia ora t ātou. What confidence does he
have that the decline in th e rate of youth who are not in  employment, education, and
training, which was announced yesterday as fa lling to 11.4 percent, is an indication that
our young people are being actively employed or are in study; and is a similar decline
being experienced by Māori?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Yes, the household labour for ce survey showed yesterday
the “neet” rate for 15 to 24- year-olds falling to 11.4 percent,  which is the lowest level
since the December quarter in 2008. That is  great to see. The number of “neet” M āori
was flat this quarter, but the Government ha s a range of initiatives that are improving
Māori employment and education outcomes—for example, M āori and Pasifika trade
training, Youth Guarantee, vocational pathways, and a focus on M āori and Pasifika
attending university, with domestic tertiary enrolments for M āori students at 21 percent
in 2012, up from 19 percent 5 years ago. I was pleased to see that, overall, M āori
employment has increased by nearly 5 percent over the last year and that unemployment
has dropped by 2.9 percent at the same time.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: How have families benefited from the Government’s economic
programme over the past 5 years?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Five years ago annual inflation for consumers was running
at more than 5 percent; it has now fallen to  a little over 1 percent.  In 2008 food prices
alone jumped 11 percent; they have gone up  by only 1.2 percent in the last year.
Floating mortgage interest rates averaged almost 11 percent in 2008; they are now less
14482 Questions for Oral Answer 7 Nov 2013
than 6 percent, although forecast to rise somewhat next year. New Zealand
superannuation payments have increased by 25 percent over the past 5 years. The tax
system has been made more progressive, reducing the proportion of net income tax paid
by those on lower incomes. Taken together, these positive indicators are helping New
Zealand families get ahead after several chal lenging years. This Government has a busy
agenda to ensure that this progress continues.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: If things were positive, would not even the most
obsequious National MP know that? So how doe s he explain the endless, repetitive
questions in the Goldsmith vein, or the interminable time he has taken—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Could the member just ask a supplementary question that is
consistent with the Standing Orders.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Well, I have and I am.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, the member has not. I will give the member one more chance;
otherwise—[Interruption] Order! If the member wants to remain in the Chamber for
question time, I will give the member one more opportunity to ask a supplementary
question that is in line with the Standing Orders.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. Would you please tell
me what was wrong with the question I was asking.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: It was unnecessarily long, it was very  hard for me to even decipher
what the question was, and it was derogatory of some National members of this House.
Would the member—[Interruption] Order! If members want to be leaving this Chamber
before the end of question time today, they wi ll be. I invite the Rt Hon Winston Peters
to ask a supplementary question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: All right. If things were pos itive, would not even the most
obsequious MP, party unnamed, know that; and how, therefore, does he explain the
endless, repetitive questions in Mr Goldsmith ’s vein, or the interminable time he is
taking to try to convince his nervous bac kbench colleagues that something positive is
happening?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I invite the Hon Steven Joyce to answer that question if there is
much ministerial responsibility.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I appreciate that the member is obsessed with the politics of
this place, but, actually, New Zealanders ou tside of this House of  Representatives are
very interested in hearing about the progress of the New Zealand economy. The member
may be bored because he has been here for so long, but, actually, the rest of the world is
very—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. He cannot possibly be
allowed to get away with that, given your restraints against my asking the question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member will resume his seat. [ Interruption] The
member will resume his seat. Otherwise he will not be remaining in the House in
question time. The member can reconsider his question in light of a question that I think
was very, very marginal. He has every right to  receive the answer he is getting from the
Hon Steven Joyce.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: What new policies is the Govern ment undertaking to continue the
positive economic momentum?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Here is an opportunity to explain to the House, including
the elderly member opposite, that I am pleased—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! On this occasion—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Order! I am on my feet. I am  on my feet. On this occasion, I
can anticipate the point of order. The Mi nister will repeat his answer without any
reference to the age of any member in this House.
7 Nov 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 14483

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: That is not my point of order.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Then I will hear the point of order, provided it is—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: The Standing Orders give me a right to raise a point of
order, particularly when an ageist inference like that one there has been slung across the
House—particularly when he is the one who has got no hair on his head.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I have just addre ssed that point of order—[ Interruption]
Order! I will not put up with a nother spurious point of order being raised by the Rt Hon
Winston Peters in this question time. The Mi nister will recommence his answer without
any reference to the age of any member in this House.

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Let me just make it clear: if members from the Government
side of the House want to stay  for the balance of question ti me—this is a point of order,
and it will be heard in silence.

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: In the past 3 days, that member has got away with slinging insults
at members in this House—th e type of insults that you would not tolerate from the
newest member of this House. Yet again, that member gets another warning—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I have not had an opportun ity to phone the member. There
was an insult cast yesterday that I think was unparliame ntary. The member Mr Horan
took objection to it. I had not heard it, but after reading Hansard the member makes a
good point. If I was to hear su ch an interjection and the member was offended, I would
deal with it appropriately. At this stage, the matter has now passed. I now invite the Hon
Steven Joyce to answer the question.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am slightly hurt at the reference to my high forehead. I am
pleased to advise that the initiatives keep  on coming. A sample of announcements that
the Government has made in just the last  few weeks include progress on work on the
Transmission Gully road, which is very impor tant, of course, in the Wellington region;
the new technology incubators to speed up company start-ups, which was announced
last week; new social housing developments for Auckland, to grow the private provision
of community housing; $260 million to suppor t the rebuild of the University of
Canterbury; the launch of the New Zealand Story, to help fi rms leverage off a strong
narrative about New Zealand’s uniqueness; proposals to bring down the cost of building
materials to support our housing supply programme; a new direction for Te Puni K ōkiri
and economic development; $30 million to de velop new schools; policy changes to
attract more international students to New Zealand; and a record $59 million in Marsden
Fund grants for top researchers. As I said, this is just a sample of our announcements
within the last couple of weeks. There ar e plenty more to come as the economy
improves.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. We were willing to listen to
such a long diatribe as long as Chorus was listed in there somewhere.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That member, as a very senior member of the Opposition,
should also stand on his feet and raise points of order that are legitimate.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: What alternative approaches would put progress in building a more
productive and competitive economy at risk?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I have given this quite a bit of thought, and there are some
alternative approaches that would put our good progress at risk, and that would cost
jobs, push up interest rates, and depress in comes. We know what those alternative
approaches are, because they have been tr ied in the past and they have failed. They
include high and wasteful Government spending, more costs and more taxes on
households and businesses, more State cont rol of the economy, a nd politicians running
everything from the electricity market to  risky insurance businesses and monetary
14484 Questions for Oral Answer 7 Nov 2013
policy. This Government rejects all these nutty old ideas that are coming from the
Greens and Labour by the day.
Sexual Assault Allegations—Confidence in Police Investigation
4. METIRIA TUREI (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Minister of Police : When was
she first advised that Police had received a complaint from a girl who alleged she had
been raped by members of a group calling themselves the Roast Busters?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: My office was advised in a phone call
from Police National Headquarters at about 5.55  last night. I was advised by my office
just after the start of the 6 o’clock news.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does the Minister share the c onfidence of the Prime Minister
regarding the police response to this case, that “If there is criminal wrongdoing that they
can follow up on and take action, then I’m abso lutely confident that they will do their
job and do it … thoroughly professionally.”, gi ven that she has now referred the police
response to that case to the Independent Police Conduct Authority?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I have made it clear in this House today that I do have
confidence in the police, but there are enough questions over this case, partly because
information has literally dribbled out this week, that have prompted me to ask the
Independent Police Conduct Authority to conduct a full investigation into  it. It is really
important that the public have confidence in  the police processes around serious sexual
assaults.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: What reasons have the police give n the Minister for waiting days to
correct the statement that was made on Sunday, that “None of the girls have been brave
enough to make formal statements to us so th at we can take that to a prosecution stage
or even consider a prosecution stage.”?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I have made it clear today how disappointed I am that
neither I nor the commissioner nor even the district commander knew that a formal
complaint had been lodged by a 13-year-old girl 2 years ago, but the commissioner does
assure me that that formal complaint wa s very thoroughly inve stigated and did not
produce enough evidence to take a case to court.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. I am not trying to make a
political point, but I did ask what reasons the police gave for fa iling to provide the
accurate information in a timely way, and that was not answered.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, I think it was. As I interp reted the answer, the question has
been asked and they are still trying to find out the reason. Th e commissioner did not
know, and he was just as concerned. The way to tease this out is by further
supplementary questions.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does the Minister consider that th e police’s apparent failure to act in
this particular case is likely to be isolated; if she does think so, why?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Again, I am assured by th e commissioner that the police
conducted a thorough investigation into the fo rmal complaint that was laid by the 13-
year-old girl and did not pr oduce enough evidence to take a case. But the very fact that
there are still questions  about the handling of this case is why I have referred it to the
Independent Police Conduct Authority to give both me and the public the assurance that
the way that the police handle these serious sexual assault cases is thorough and is in
line with the new protocols, and to give us all an assurance that this is an isolated case.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: What advice has the Minister sought on removing the systemic
barriers that prevent the police from taking comp laints to trial, which lead the police to
wait for more assaults on young girls to occur, as has happened in this case, for some
years before they believe they have sufficient evidence to take the case to trial?
7 Nov 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 14485

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Again, the commissioner assures me that there has been a
very thorough investigation, a nd that that investigation has been ongoing for 2 years,
trying to put together enough ev idence to meet the requirement s to take a case to court.
As recently as 2 weeks ago, the other three girls were approached by police to try to get
a formal complaint from them. In two cas es their mothers refused, and, again, the
commissioner advises me that the third girl has also refu sed. No one underestimates the
difficulties for these young girls in making a formal complaint, but the police have done
an enormous amount of work, and I refer the member to the protocol s that were tabled
by the Minister of Justice in the House ear lier this week. They were worked through
with Louise Nicholas, who was involved in a very notable case. She has worked very
closely with police from a vict im’s perspective. What I want to be able to assure New
Zealanders, through an Independent Polic e Conduct Authority report into this
investigation, and, in particular, into the investigation around the case of this young 13-
year-old girl, is that all t hose protocols were followed, th e victim was at the centre of
the investigation, and New Zeal anders can have confidence in the police in order to
come forward and make these complaints.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Will the Minister support the urge nt development of a specialist
sexual violence court and an alternative pro cess for sexual violence offence cases, both
of which have received very strong suppor t from judges, lawyers, sexual violence
support services, and the public, given the diffi culties that victims have bringing their
complaints to the police, the difficulties the police have in dealing sensitively and
responsively with those complaints, and the police’s reluctance to take sexual violence
cases to trial?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: First of all, I have no mini sterial responsibility for the
development of such a policy, but I have disc ussed it with the Minister of Justice, who
addressed it in this House earlier this w eek. These cases are extremely complex. One of
the difficulties is trying to se parate out a particular set of  charges around these assault
cases in order to try them in a different way from some of the other aspects of that case,
in which case you would be putting your victims through the process twice, which is a
difficult enough process anyway without re victimising a person and making them go
through two lots of courts. It is ongoing. The Minister of Justice has made it clear that
she is willing to talk with the police and he r department about some ways of easing the
process for these young women, but these are very difficult cases to take to court and to
prove.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Will the Minister commit to leading a cross-party working group to
build both a political consensu s and also political urgency for the reforms of the court
and police processes, such as a specialist sexual violence court and changes to police
process, to better deliver real justice to the victims of sexual violence offences,
particularly children—as in this case—and better justice for their families and New
Zealanders?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Again, I repeat that I have no ministerial responsibility. I
cannot make that guarantee. But what I have sa id, to try to explain to this House today,
is that the police have made enormous change s to the way that they deal with sexual
assault cases, and victims in particular. I would like the Independent Police Conduct
Authority to investigate this case to give me reassurance, and to give the public
reassurance, that as much as we can do—and will continue to do—has been put into
practice by the police in this instance. Bu t if the member and her party have any
suggestions about how we can ease this proces s while still retaining the need to have
evidence to take to court, I would be delighted to hear it.
14486 Questions for Oral Answer 7 Nov 2013
Broadband, Ultra-fast—Infrastructure Pricing and Contract with Chorus
5. Hon DAVID PARKER (Deputy Leader—Labour)  to the Minister for

items.speaker: Communications and Information Technology
items.text: Will the Government enforce its
broadband contract with Chorus?
Hon AMY ADAMS (Minister for Communications and Information
Technology): As I have previously st ated, the Government expect s all parties to fulfil
their contractual obligations with the Govern ment. The contract with Chorus contains a
number of enforcement options if it were to fail to meet its obligations. The concern for
the Government is ensuring that New Zeala nders get ultra-fast broadband to deliver
high-quality, high-speed, world-leading telecommunications. That is our focus in this
issue, and our consideration of options will be guided by the best way to achieve that.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Why was an independent review of the financial viability of
Chorus not undertaken prior to awarding the broadband contract to Chorus?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: Although I would take issue with that, I can assure the member
that considerable due diligence was done th rough the contract negotiations into the
capability of parties to undertake the obligat ions. What we have said consistently
through this is that although there was an understanding that the copper price may well
fall, nobody expected a price drop of this level and none of the pricing methodologies,
therefore, would have work ed through such an unanticip ated drop. I would point out
that that failure to antici pate such a drop was shared by members of the Labour Party
who, as I recall, actively pr edicted that the copper pr ice would rise under these
arrangements.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Will this latest review examine th e role of Mr Joyce, the former
Minister for Communications and Information Technology, in crafting the legislation
and awarding the contract to Chorus?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: The independent stream of advi ce that I have asked for today
is about ensuring that the Government and the wider community have good information
as to whether or not having the copper price set at this level would seriously undermine
and threaten New Zealanders’ ab ility to get ultra-fast broa dband. That is certainly the
indication that we have had, but some peopl e, including some members in this House,
have suggested that that is  not right. We need good information to back up whether or
not—as we suspect, and as the advice we have  had says—that would put it at risk. That
is what this review is about.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speak er. That is all very interesting,
but it was not my question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I heard the question. The difficulty I had was actually in
hearing the answer accurately because of  the noise coming from Opposition benches
here. If the member has further supplementa ry questions, that is the way to get the
answer he wants.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. If the Speaker could not
hear the answer and therefore could not j udge whether the questi on was addressed, the
Speaker should have brought the House into order. My point of order was that I did hear
the answer and my question was not addressed.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: In the bits of the answer I hear d, because it was difficult to hear, I
believe the question was addressed—maybe not to the member’s satisfaction. But it
would certainly assist if the deputy leader of  the Labour Party could ask for his party to
support him so that when he asks a questi on, the question can be answered without a
level of interjection [ Interruption]—Order! [ Interruption] There is not much point in
looking behind yourself. It would certainly be assisted if we  had a level of interjection
7 Nov 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 14487
that was substantially less than what is occurring on this particular day, mainly from the
Labour Opposition benches.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. I have some difficulty in
being told that my point of order is out of  order because the Speaker could not hear the
answer to assess whether the question was addr essed, and then be told that that is my
fault.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member maybe misheard me or maybe misunderstood
me. I said I did not hear all of the answer because of the level of interjection. I asked for
the member’s assistance with his colleagues to try to minimise the level of interjection. I
then said that although I did not hear all of the answer, what I did hear of it led me to
believe that the question had been addressed. I accept that it may not be to the
satisfaction of the member, but the way forwar d is not to raise a point of order saying
that the question has not been answered the way the member wanted it to be answered.
The way forward is for the member to rise  to his feet and as k a further searching
supplementary question.

items.speaker: Clare Curran
items.text: Will her review announced today include examination of whether
any private or other assuran ces were given to parent company Telecom and/or Chorus
during the demerger and ultra-fast broadba nd tendering processes that led them to
believe that there would not be a fall in copper prices; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: The review is not my review. I have asked for an independent
review to be provided to the Government, wh ich I have indicated I will release to the
public. What that will look at is whether Chor us is reasonably able to be expected to
complete its contractual obligations to provide ultra-fast broadband. That is what it will
look at. It will not go into any Opposition conspiracy theories.

items.speaker: Clare Curran
items.text: How has her decision to undertake a narrow, specific, and possibly
illegal review of the 2011 amendment to th e Telecommunications Act 3 years before it
was due—bypassing the Commerce Commission’s legal proce ss of reviewing copper
broadband pricing—created more certainty; and is  it not so that her tactics between last
December and now have failed, resulting in grea ter uncertainty about the future of both
Chorus and the Government’s flagship ultra-fast broadband process?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: Well, firstly, I reject most of the allegations in that member’s
question, and, secondly, no and no.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Why is the Government creati ng investment uncertainty for
other investors in telecommunication compan ies, and what measures has she put in
place to ensure that the review is not just a snow job to justify more corporate welfare or
higher copper broadband prices?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: Well, it seems to me that ju st yesterday the Opposition was
demanding an independent look into the affairs and numbers of Chorus. Actually, that is
something that I signalled 2 days earlier that  we were going to do. That is what we are
now doing. So is it the Opposition’s posi tion that we should not actually ask
independent questions? Regardless, we make decisions—

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: Yeah, nah, yeah, nah.

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: That is right. We are not the “Yeah, Nah Party” on this side.
We make decisions based on information an d analysis. Where that information is
challenged and we think it is a matter of significant public interest, as this is, we are
happy to get further independent analysis and we are happy to release that publicly. This
will help inform the debate and get New Z ealanders focused on the question of whether
this copper price—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The answer is now getting a bit long.
14488 Questions for Oral Answer 7 Nov 2013
Freshwater Management—Reform
6. CLAUDETTE HAUITI (National) to the Minister for the Environment: What
announcements has the Government made in relation to the national policy statement
for freshwater?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: Today my colleague the
Minister for Primary Industries, Nathan Guy, and I released proposals for improving the
way New Zealand manages its fresh water,  including science-backed national water
standards, which were a key recommendation of the Land and Water Forum. Ensuring
that we protect and improve water quality now  and for the future is one of our most
critical challenges. The discussion document we have released seeks feedback on a
national framework to support communities se tting freshwater objectives, explicit
recognition of tangata whenua values for fr esh water, ecosystem and human health as
compulsory values in regional plans, bo ttom lines for those values, and requiring
councils to account for all water takes and all contaminant discharges into water bodies.

items.speaker: Claudette Hauiti
items.text: What is the purpose of the national objectives framework?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: The national objectives framework will provide regions with
both a process and a scientifically informed  basis for the difficult communications and
conversations that communities are having to  have on water quality. When combined
with the Government’s already announced  collaborative planning process option and
better water accounting, it is our hope that th e framework will result in more informed
discussions in communities about the trade-offs, and reduce the arguments in councils
and in courts over the science that sits behind regional plans and resource consents.

items.speaker: Meka Whaitiri
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Speaker. Why does her Proposed amendments to the
National Policy Statement fo r Freshwater Management  contain incomplete standards
and standards lower than current levels, when  the lack of clear bottom-lines was a core
issue highlighted by the Land and Water Forum?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: We have been very clear that the work around completing the
table and the values to be attributed for each attribute is ongoing. The science work is
still being completed, but the scientists have been very clear, as has the reference group,
that we need to start with the informa tion we have. We are not going to wait an
interminable number of years, as the Labour  Government did. We are going to start to
improve water quality today, and I can assure this House and the member who asked the
question that the level at which those botto m lines have been set—and they are bottom
lines; they are not targets—is the level at  which 60 of New Zealand’s top scientists
agreed was the appropriate place to set them.

items.speaker: Te Ururoa Flavell
items.text: T ēnā t ātou. How have the rights and responsibilities of Ng āti
Kahungunu as tangata whenua in Hawke’s Ba y been recognised, given that both the
National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management and the Ruataniwha Dam
project have been dealt with by the Government at a national level and not at a regional
or local level?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: To the best of my recollect ion, in the instance of the
Ruataniwha Dam application it was the regional council of th at area that requested that
the application be dealt with through a national Environmental Protection Authority
process. So that has come from the region. The other point I would make to the member
is that, of course, that de termination is being made under the current framework, and
this is about how we improve that going forward. I can certainly advise the member that
one of the key messages we took from commu nity consultation was the integration of
tangata whenua values within the national obj ectives framework. Te mana o te wai is a
core principle of the document. You will see values such as the mahinga kai use of
water and wāi tapu clearly reflected in the framew ork. When you combine that with the
7 Nov 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 14489
increased and enhanced integrated role of  iwi in the planning process, I think Ng āti
Kahungunu and other iwi can be satisfied that th ey will have a much greater level of
involvement in such decisions in the future.
Housing Market—Impact of Reserve Bank Intervention
7. PHIL TWYFORD (Labour—Te Atat ū) to the Minister of Housing : What
reports has he re ceived on the effect of loan-to- value restrictions on the housing
market?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I have not rece ived any formal
reports, and the advice from my officials is that after just 1 mont h it is too early to
draw firm conclusions on the effect of the loan-to-valu e ratio restri ctions on the
housing market. I ha ve noted three report s from other sources. The first is from
Statistics New Zealand on buildi ng consents . It showed a 22 perc ent increase in new
dwelling consents, as compared  with the same month last year; the highest  build rate
in Canterbury in 37 year s; and the highest build rate for New Zealand in 5 years. I also
note the latest real es tate figures on house prices, which show a sl owing in house price
increases, and a report from  the ASB showing a dip in house price expectations. The
final report I note states: “We do support Loan to Va lue Ratios…we’ve been calling
for them for ages,”. This report was from  Mr Phil Twyford.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Is he concerned that Master Builders said that inquiries for new
builds have dropped off by 30 percent since loan-t o-value ratios were  introduced, and
that because of the time lag it will not be until next year that we see the drop-off in
new builds; if so, is this not just more evidence that the Government’s housing policy
has collapsed?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: It is hard to say that it ha s collapsed when we have got the
highest rate of new bu ilding consents in 5 years, when we have got the highest rate of
building in Canterbury in 37 years, and when this Government  has got work under
way on materials, on land  supply, and on infrastruct ure costs—all opposed by
members opposite, who somehow pretend that they want to  help New Zealanders to
get access to a ffordable houses.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Has he seen the comments by Qu otable Value research director
Jonno Ingerson, who sa id today that loan-to-value rati os may have more impact in
provincial areas outsid e of Auckland and Canterbury; and given that 95 percent of
house price inflation is taki ng place in Auckland and Cant erbury, and that in a number
of parts of provincial New Zealand house prices  are either static or  declining, will he
concede that the Government really did not thi nk through the implic ations of loan-to-
value ratios before it signed off the agreement with the Reserve Bank?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The Hon Dr Nick Smith, in so  far as he ha s ministerial
responsibility.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The first point is that the loan-to-value ratio policy has
been implemented by an in dependent Reserve Ba nk, under legislat ion that members
opposite actually support, I thought—an indepe ndent Reserve Bank . The part that
makes the member’s question even more stupid is that he has said on the public record
that he has been calling for loan-to-value ratios for years and welcomed them when
they were introduced.

items.speaker: Louise Upston
items.text: What has been the average house price increase over the past 5
years and how did it compare with the increase over the pr evious 5 years?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The average price in crease in New Zeala nd over the last 5
years has been 3.6 percent per year, or 20 pe rcent over those 5 years. It is interesting
to note that in the previous 5 years it in creased by an average of  12 percent per year,
14490 Questions for Oral Answer 7 Nov 2013
or 76 percent in just 5 years,  and I note that du ring the previous 5 years the Labour
Government did absolutely di ddly-squat about house price affordability. In contrast,
we are making great progress in  all the areas like land supply, infrastructure costs, and
materials, and, ironically , members opposite are opp osing every one of those
measures.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: When he compared our mortgage market with that of the United
States, which saw “millions of  Americans left with mortga ges in excess of the value
of their properties.”, what advice has he had to back up his claim that Auckland is in a
housing price bubb le and that it is in danger of bursting, wipi ng out the equity built up
by homeowners?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I do think that this  country needs to learn the lessons from
both North America and Europe, where, for all the enth usiasm there may have been
from the building industries , those house price bubbles did enormous  damage to those
economies. I cannot beli eve the attitude of members oppo site, which is to completely
ignore the lessons of history and not want to take a ca utious view around financial
stability in the way in which our Reserve Bank is administ ering those resp onsibilities.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: I raise a point of orde r, Mr Speaker. I referred the Minister to a
direct quote from his own st atement and I asked him what advice he has received on
that matter. He di d not address that.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: To make progress, I am going to  invite the member to ask his
question again.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: When he compared our mortgage market with that of the United
States, which saw “millions of  Americans left with mortga ges in excess of the value
of their properties.”, what advi ce has he had to ba ck up the claim that Auckland is in a
housing price bubb le and that it is in danger of bursting, wipi ng out the equity built up
by homeowners?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: It is an absolute matter of public record, with numerous
reports, that New Zeal and’s house prices ar e grossly out of step with incomes. The
most recent report was yest erday, from the OECD. We c ould look at the reports from
Labour’s period in Government, when house prices more than d oubled—grew by over
100 percent—at the same time as incomes went up by only 30 percent. We could look
at the report of the Produc tivity Commission, which was comprehens ive in its advice
around the concern about ongo ing house price increases,  and that is why this
Government is addressing the fundamentals of land suppl y, infrastructure costs, and
materials costs to make sure that New Ze alanders get access to more affordable
housing.

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: Is the Minister aware of a coll apse in the number of first-home
buyer inquiries in Tauranga a nd Nelson since the loan-to-va lue restrictions came into
force; and did he foresee this, or is it an unintended consequence?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: On 1 October this Government actually increased the
support for first-home buyers. We did th at by expanding the KiwiSaver scheme,
which was particularly advantageous for pe ople in Nelson and Tauranga, where the
house price limit was lifted by over $50,000 . We have trebled th e number of Welcome
Home Loans, which are limi ted to first-home buyers a nd provide them with an
exemption from those loan-to-value limits from the Reserve Bank, and those changes
to Welcome Home Loans are particularly he lpful for communities like Tauranga and
Nelson, because the previous limits meant that very few families had access to those
Welcome Home Loans.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Does he have the same attitude to the plight of  first-home buyers
shut out of the Kiwi dream by high loan-to- value restrictions as  that of the Prime
7 Nov 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 14491
Minister, who told them in the New Zealand Herald  today: “ ‘yeah, okay, well fine’.
That’s the way it goes.”?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The Prime Minister has been absolutely committed to
first-home buyers. That is w hy this Government, as I ha ve just said, trebled the
number of Welcome Home Loans and double d the number of people who will be
eligible for the KiwiSaver firs t-home deposit subsidy, and it is why the Prime Minister
is such a strong supporter of  this Government’s very am bitious agenda to get house
prices under control after a period of Government und er Labour, where those house
prices more than doubled.
Beneficiaries—Statistics
8. Hon PHIL HEATLEY (National—Whangarei)  to the Minister for Social

items.speaker: Development
items.text: What reports has she re ceived about the number of people receiving
benefits?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I have received a
report that shows that at the quarter ending  in September, the num ber of people on a
working-age benefit has reduced  by 16,500 people ov er the last year. To put this in
context, at the height of the global financ ial crisis in January 2010, there were more
than 347,000 people on a benefit. There are now just over 304,000.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Heatley
items.text: What does the report to the Minister show about long-term
welfare dependence, though?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: The investment approach is beginning to tackle the
issue of long-term  dependence on welfar e and it is also one of our Better Public
Services targets. The report shows that 87 percent of the people who came off the
benefit in the year ended Se ptember 2013 had been on a bene fit for longer than a year.
This is crucial because, of course, the longer you are on  a benefit, the more you are
likely to become depe ndent in the long term.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Heatley
items.text: How is Work and Income better as sisting those at risk of long-
term welfare dependence?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: We have more staff, who ar e able to help more people.
To give you an example, befo re the introduction of these welfare reforms they saw an
average of about 2,000 people per week. They  are now working wi th more like 15,000
people per week. That means we can get the support in ear lier, look at beneficiaries’
barriers to work, and, of course, see outstanding results for New Zealanders.
Industry Training—Under-representation of Women
9. CAROL BEAUMONT (Labour)  to the Minister for Tertiary Education,

items.speaker: Skills and Employment
items.text: How does women’s participat ion rate of 1 percent in
building and construction indu stry training assist with  the Christchurch rebuild?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for Tertiary Education, Skills and
Employment): I think all participation is helpful in  the rebuild. It wo uld, of course, be
good to see more women involv ed in building a nd construction in Canterbury. There
is, of course, no practical limit on the num ber of female buildin g and construction
trades apprenticeships. There are places  available right now and I would welcome
more women to consider taki ng up those career opportunities.  It is worth noting that
the proportion of female indu stry trainees has been tren ding upwards over the last 7
years. It was 31 percent in 2012. The proportion of female trainees in the five key
building, construction, and in frastructure industry traini ng organisations is also
trending upwards around the country, includi ng in Canterbury, although it has to be
said that this is off a low base.
14492 Questions for Oral Answer 7 Nov 2013

items.speaker: Carol Beaumont
items.text: How does a woman’s participation rate of 4 percent in the
boatbuilding industry, 5 percen t in the infrastructure indu stry, or 7 pe rcent in the
electrical supply indust ry help with the Better Public Services goal of  increasing the
number of people with advanc ed trades qualifications?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: It is true that in some areas women have less participation
in training; in other areas the rates are higher —for example, in the area of un iversities
and tertiary education genera lly more women are involved than me n. You cannot say
that that is necessarily a bad thing, but there are in itiatives that we ca n take. It is good
that the member raises th e Electricity Supply Indust ry Training Organisation. The
organisation has got more in itiatives. One is called Ulti mit and encourages women to
apply for trade and technical roles in their s ector. There are things like the Top Female
Trade Student Award at Chri stchurch Polytechnic Instit ute of Technology, which was
announced today too. Th at is also designed to raise th e profile of wome n in trades.

items.speaker: Carol Beaumont
items.text: What initiatives has he  put in place to lift the participation rate
of women in industry trai ning, which has decreased from  30 percent in 2010 to 28
percent in 2013, noting that he  conveniently talked  only about 2012?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: My records here are 31 perc ent in 2012. But the member
makes a very interesting point.  I do think it is fair that  we consider more policy
options, because as well as trying to lift the participation of wo men, we could perhaps
restrict the participation of  men until the participation of women gets to the same
level. I think that is what is colloquially known as a man ban. I think that could be a
way in which we  could achieve—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order! That answer is not going to help you.
[Interruption] Order! Is there a supplementary question?

items.speaker: Carol Beaumont
items.text: Getting back to the matter in hand—[ Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Carol Beaumont
items.text: How successful does he believe the initiatives he has worked on
with the Ministry of Women’ s Affairs, like the research  project showing there is a
pool of women available to as sist in the Canterbury rebuil d or the research following

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: This bill is the
innocuously named the New Zealand Internatio nal Convention Centre Bill. It sounds
like a lovely idea, except it is not the right title. The correct title here is the “Skycity
Crony Capitalism (Looking After Their Mates by the National Party) Bill”, because that
is what this bill should be called. We have just been voting through the schedules—

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: That’s a long title.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: That is a long title. Long ti tles also were got rid of 20
years ago, Mr Goff. But if we were actually to  look at the schedules that we have just
been voting on, we would see that they contain the guts of what is in  this agreement. It
is important, in what I suspect will be one of my final contributi ons on this bill, to
actually remind members of the public what it is  that is being given away here. What is
being given away here is a massive extension out to 2048 to the licence for Skycity.
Within that period the two reviews required under the Gambling Act are dispensed with.
Secondly, we have an additional 230 single terminal gaming machines. We have an
additional 240 automated gaming table termin als. We have an additional 12 further
gaming tables. We have the introduction of  cashless gaming machines. We have the
7 Nov 2013 New Zealand Internatio nal Convention Centre Bill 14499
ticket-in, ticket-out provisions , which have been put up by the officials as having the
possibility of allowing for money-laundering.  Those are the concessions. Those are the
things that in this bill mean that the title is inappropriate because they directly contradict
the Gambling Act.
They are the things that make this bill no t about an international convention centre,
but about crony capitalism—about one firm , one company in New Zealand, being
treated differently from the rest of the co mpanies in New Zealand. That started on the
very first day. That started when the Prim e Minister wrote on t op of the officials’
briefing note “Cover off the Skycity angle.” At that moment the crony capitalism button
was pushed and the Government’s officials went  off into a separate line of negotiations
with Skycity. Skycity then got more inform ation about the proces s than other bidders
did. It was invited to put in proposals that ot her bidders were not invited to put in place.
At that point the process was rorted, th e process was wrong, and that was at the
direction of John Key, the Prime Minister —the crony capitalist in chief, John Key—
who came across the top of a process to bu ild an international convention centre in
Auckland, and did a deal. He did a dodgy deal. He is up to his neck in it, and that should
be reflected in the title of this bill. So that is the first step at which things went wrong.
Then the legislation to do this was introdu ced in the House, and I spoke about it last
night. In clause 6(2) of this bill we have the sight of the Nationa l Government deciding
to override the laws of this land via its  dodgy, backroom deal. The Gambling Act and
associated gambling legisla tion is ridden roughshod over by this law. This is no
ordinary piece of law coming to this House; it is a law that justifies the Government’s
dodgy backroom deals. It rides roughshod ove r other legislation, and it puts in place
concessions that go against the Gambling Act.
There is no doubt whatsoever that gambling harm will be increased by this
legislation. The Government has actuall y acknowledged that, by not amending the
Gambling Act where its purpose is to reduce gambling harm. It cannot do that, because
this bill increases gambling harm. Up to 5,000 extra problem gamblers will be created
as a result of this, with all the flow-on effects thr ough our communities, through
families and through people who face the horrible addiction that is class 4 gambling, in
particular, on the pokie machines. This is a bill that has the potential to increase money-
laundering through Skycity. It introduces types of gambling that across the world have
seen increases in problem gambling.
This bill should not be before this House. This bill goes against the principles that
New Zealanders believe in—about how laws should be made and that a Government
will actually look after its citizens. The Gove rnment is not here to do deals with its
mates; the Government is here to protect Ne w Zealand citizens and ensure that they can
go about their daily lives, knowing that the Government is there for them. We might not
agree with every single thing th at the party opposite does, but wh at we expect is that it
will bring legislation to this House that s upports and protects the rights of New Zealand
citizens. That is not what the Government  has done here. It has brought a piece of
legislation to this House that favours one company, and that goes against the values of
New Zealanders. It is a shameful piece of legislation.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Chairperson. T ēnā koutou
e te Whare. This legislation, the New Zeala nd International Convention Centre Bill, is
before the House only because the Governme nt needs to exclude Skycity from the
Gambling Act. Do you remember that th e Gambling Act expresses an absolute
prohibition on the creation of any further cas inos and on the expansion in any way of
existing casinos? Skycity has, for some decades now, been fighting the Gambling
Commission on its decision to refuse Skycity  further licences to expand its business.
What Skycity has done through this deal is  find an alternative way to get round the
14500 New Zealand International C onvention Centre Bill 7 Nov 2013
gambling law, because the gambling law has stopped it from expanding as it would like.
It is not like Skycity does not make a huge amount of money—it makes huge profits, in
any event. It is just gree d, frankly. This legislation should not be called the New
Zealand International Convention Centre Bill, at all. It is the “Skycity Greed Bill”.
It is the “Skycity (Third-largest Casino in the Country Delivery Device) Bill”. That is
what this actually is. I do not know whether people will remember in the past, around
the time of the smoke-free - tobacco inquiry, that cigarettes were described as “nicotine-
delivery devices”. I do not know whether you remember that—nicotine-delivery devices
are what cigarettes are. That is why this legi slation and this Skycity deal is essentially a
casino-delivery device to Skycity. There w ould be no legislation in this Committee if
there were not this deal, which funds th e building of a convention centre through the
gambling concessions, and if there were not  the need to get round the Gambling Act.
Part of the reason why this bill is stru ctured as it is—rather than amending the
Gambling Act, for example—is simply that the Government did not want to have the
public understand clearly enough and openly that  the whole point of this deal was to
give Skycity a legislative way of avoidi ng the constraints a nd the public health
regulations in the Gambling Act.
There are, what, 23 pages of words in this bill, but if you took out  all of those parts
that are related to the Gambling Act and the concessions, you are talking about only five
provisions—maybe a few more; maybe seven provisions—that ar e at all related to the
convention centre itself because very little of this deal requires any legislative changes.
There is a little bit around the flags—the Flags, Emblems, and Name Protection Act—
and there is a little bit around the name of the conventio n centre, but essentially this
entire bill is designed to give Skycity a mechanism to get round the Gambling Act. That
is because Skycity has wanted for years to significantly expand its business, and now it
can. Now what it has is the third-largest casino being delivered to it by John Key.
The Green Party constructed for members of  Parliament and their policy people, on
the Tuesday just gone, an almost life-sized  replica of the extra 230 pokie machines, 240
automated gaming terminals, and 12 gaming tables out here on the parliamentary lawns,
so that when MPs came to vote this bill and exercise their consciences, they would
understand exactly what they were voting for. They are not voting for a convention
centre. It does not need legi slation. They are voting for the reality that that cardboard
casino confronted MPs with. It was huge. It took up almost th e entirety of the grass out
the front of Parliament. The pokie machines  had messages from Aucklanders written on
them saying: “Please do not pass this bill . Please do not cause my family and friends
and my community any more harm.”—genuine  pleas to members of Parliament, who
have a choice on whether to deliver the third- largest casino to Skycity or not. Part of
that choice will be made today in the votes that each individual MP will cast.
The concessions that have been granted have  been laid out. They are extraordinary.
We are talking about nearly one extra prob lem gambler being created as a result of
every single pokie machine that will be established, so there will be around 200 extra
problem gamblers, an estimated 8,000 bei ng individuals affect ed by that problem
gambling, and an extra 6,500 children being affected by that problem gambling. The
impact of this legislation—w hich is gambling legislation, make no mistake—is that a
significant proportion of New Zealanders will be harmed.
What we know from all of the papers that  have been released so far—and, frankly,
not every piece of advice has been released—i s that the economics of this do not stack
up. So the Government’s argument that somehow  Skycity is entitled to the extensive,
third-largest casino in the country because  somewhere else down the track it will
contribute to economic development in New Zealand has been proved false. The only
independent report that has been done on any of the economics of this issue showed that
7 Nov 2013 New Zealand Internatio nal Convention Centre Bill 14501
there will be a net creati on across the country of 18 j obs—just 18 jobs. Although there

it is another kind of convention centre—

items.speaker: Louisa Wall
items.text: Let the market pay for it.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: That is right. Even if a conve ntion centre does provide limited
economic development, is it, none the less, a wise thing to have for other parts of the

Government not choose an ethi cal means to fund th e building of a conve ntion centre in
Auckland? If the Auckland Council thinks it is a good idea, it s hould put in some
money. If the Government thinks it is a good idea, it should put in some money. If the

different ways of funding this thing that do not  require the cost of it to be borne on the
backs of problem gamblers. Maybe that is wh at we should call this bill—this is the
“Problem Gamblers Pay for the New Zeala nd International Convention Centre Bill”.
Maybe that would be a more honest title for th is legislation, because if it were not for
the fact that Skycity is getting the concessi ons as a result of this deal, we would not
have this legislation before us today.
Most of it could be done by an agreement by the Government in a public-private
partnership, whether we like it or not. You know, it would not be the end of the world if
the Government was doing a deal with Skycit y and it was an economic deal that did not

at least it would be morally explainable. Bu t at the moment what we have here is
morally contemptible. It is a morally contemptible piece of legislation that every single
MP will be putting their name to if they vote for it.

items.speaker: Louisa Wall
items.text: Only them.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: That is right. If you vote for th is legislation, you are voting for
morally contemptible legislation. You are vo ting for more children being left in the
Skycity car park.

items.text: That is a presumption, Mr Goff, but I am an eternal optimist and
I want to believe in the best in people. I want to believe th at the Parliament to which I

decisions based on rational ar gument, evidence, and the best  interests of the people of

We could call this bill all sorts of things . I have tried to call the whole deal some

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: I just want to carry on from where my
colleague from the Greens, Metiria Turei, left  off because I completely agree with her.
The New Zealand International Convention Ce ntre Bill is a bill that is improperly
named. It should be the “Look After Your Mates (Sleazy C onvention Centre) Bill.” I
hope I am able to stay in the Chamber after saying that title.
At the end of the day, this whole bill is built so lely around the fact that we have to
bring in changes to our gambling laws in order to get this convention centre up. If it was
just a simple convention centre,  we would not have to be do ing this. If it was a simple
deal that did not involve a shonky deal, we w ould not have to be doing this either. As
the Deputy Auditor-General said, it was flawed , it was not transparent, and there were
deficiencies on the part of Ministers and thei r officials. When the Prime Minister said
that he was totally vindicated by her report, she said: “No, that isn’t the case at all.” In
fact, she said: “You don’t have to spend time writing 40 or 50 pages of an Auditor-
General’s report if he was going to be totally vindicated.”
This was a deal that was shonky from the beginning because of the way it was
carried out. It was done over dinner. It was done through  a whole bunch of secret
meetings between the Prime Minister’s offi ce and Skycity. It cut out completely the
other four tenderers that wanted to have a l ook in to this bill as well. They did not get a
good look in. Instead, we had Skycity and, in stead, we had to amend massive amounts
of legislation in order for S kycity to get the cosy deal th at it ended up with. Otherwise
we would not have needed to do it.
What sort of deal did Skycity end up w ith? Well, the curren t 110 gambling tables
will go up by 40—by 40. And listen to this: Skycity has 1,657 pokie machines
currently—1,657 currently in operation—and it is going to lift that by 230 more. But
here is the kicker in this—here is the kicker: what Skycity will get out of this is not just
the extra pokie machines but also 359 of those pokie machines will have their limits
lifted from $20 to $100. They will have in-out cards, so you do not ac tually have to put
any money in whatsoever.
This is designed to fleece those people who cannot afford to put their money in these
pokie machines in the first place, faster than th ey have ever done before. It will increase
gambling harm much more than has occurred in  the past. This is a bill designed to give
Skycity an enormous shot in the arm. I asked a former employee of Skycity whom I
spoke to before this came forward about what so rt of deal this would be, and he laid out
what he thought it would be. He was surprise d—he was surprised that Skycity got such
a great deal.
This will not enhance New Zealand’s reputation. It will not be the economic
development miracle that Steven Joyce said  it would be. It will  pull money out of
people who can least afford that money and it will put money in the pockets of those
people in New Zealand who have already got  that money. This is wrong. It will do
nothing for New Zealand except provide the k nowledge that our convention centre is
being built on the backs of people who can leas t afford to pay for it. We, the taxpayers,
will be paying the bill for all of those thousands of New Zealanders, their families, and
their kids who will be poorer as a result of this shonky piece of legislation. Here we are
in this Chamber on a Thursday afternoon deba ting a bill that should never have come to
7 Nov 2013 New Zealand Internatio nal Convention Centre Bill 14503
this House because we should have had a pr oper process that would have enabled other
companies to have a fair look in to the situation.

The title of this bill, the New Zealand Inte rnational Convention Centre Bill, in clause

a little unusual to you, but it is actually refl ective of what this bi ll is about. Was this a
bill simply to implement the result of a competitive tender to build the convention
centre? No, it was not. There was no tender.  There was no competitive bidding. This is
a deal where John Key sat down and was wined and dined by Skycity and gave it a
gold-plated deal. This is the wide boy, curr ency trader way of reaching a deal. It has
nothing to do with the propriety of public sector tendering.

items.speaker: There were other tenderers out there
items.text: Vector and Ngāti Whātua. They were reputable

above-board way without the dishonesty and th e dirty dealing that this bill represents.
But that process never happened. John Key had two personal meetings. He told his

items.speaker: The Auditor-General looked at  this and though t
items.text: “I’d better cons ider what has
happened here. It doesn’t seem right.” Just before she was due to report, John Key came
out and said that the report would totally vindicate him. That was another piece of

Government should be behaving, said that there were deficienci es on the part of
Ministers, deficiencies on the part of offici als. In fact, she said this about it: “we do not
consider that the evaluation process was tr ansparent or even ha nded.” That was the
considered language of an Auditor-General. Anybody else would have said that that was

I want to say this. The title I suggested  is an alternative title—the “Convention
Centre (Dirty Deal Implementation) Bill”—but there is another title that would be more
honest than what this Government is hidi ng behind. It is the “Increasing Harm from
Gambling Bill”, because how was the Gove rnment going to fund this convention

What has the Government actually done? It is funding this  by increasing the

Because the regulatory impact statement from the officials for this bill said that this

What we find from the regulatory impact statement is that the Department of Internal

I will try one third and last ti tle that this bill should be  called, and that is the “Dodgy

Of course, this bill is a gold-plated deal  for Skycity to make money until 2048. Most

protect and enhance the position of its cronies. The legislati on is a disgrace. It should
not proceed. It is damaging to New Zealand, it looks after the cronies, and the process
that this National Government has followed in pursuing it is, frankly, a disgrace.
